utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we have a visitor in the courtroom today, Judge Rant from the United Kingdom. He is the Judge Advocate General, senior judge presiding over courts marshal in the United Kingdom. The Judge sits in court by agreement of the parties, and I take it that there is no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No objection, and we welcome him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. What is the position now about the witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was intended to call, on this Monday afternoon and possibly Wednesday afternoon, two witnesses, the first of whom was a particularly confidential witness whose details were only disclosed a fortnight ago. That witness and the other witness were due to travel together, I think, on Saturday. In the event, the confidential witness did not travel, was not available to travel, but at the moment I don't know precisely why not. Probably it's the case that he was beset by fears and anxieties. There are a number of people in that area like him who are compelled to return to homes from which they were forced to go, and by reason of that return, they find themselves back amongst people of a different ethnic background from them, and therefore they find themselves more anxious, perhaps, than they had been where they had been living meanwhile. So that's probably the reason, but I can say no more about it than that. He hasn't, to my knowledge, been spoken to directly since he failed to travel on Saturday, although, of course, steps are in hand to ensure that he should be spoken to. I should have asked for private session and I'm not sure that I did, but I haven't named anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have a witness here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll need to deal with that witness first in private session as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May we have private session for the remainder of what I'm saying about the confidential witness and the other witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In April 1992, at the lodge you've already mentioned, did soldiers arrive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many, and by whom were they led?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were about 25 or 26, I don't know the exact number, and they were led by Cerkez. He was the commander of these troops. That's what he was addressed as.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you known Cerkez before the conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from his birth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Without using any names that will identify you, what did Cerkez say to you about what was happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came in the morning, around 8.00, and he first approached me and told me as follows: "Lady, there's no more work. There will be no more business here. This is now our facility. We have come here to carry out exercises, and we will stay here, I don't know how long, until we are given orders to move on, and you cannot work here any longer. You have to leave, that is, you can stay but you cannot do any business any longer. You cannot have any guests."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What arms did Cerkez or the soldiers have with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They had rifles. Cerkez had a pistol, that is, at the time when they entered the motel, and the others also had weapons. There were three or maybe four, I saw about three trucks, and they had mortars on them and other weapons which they were going to use for their exercises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ask what you should do about your loss of a living? If so, what were you told?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I asked Mr. Cerkez who was going to compensate me for all the effort. I had just cleaned up; I had just brought in new supplies, had them delivered on a truck for my work. He said, "Lady, don't worry. Whoever wins will pay you," and I said, "What kind of a victory is to be expected here? There is no fighting here," and he said, "You will hear about it in due time. You don't need to know now."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Eventually, did you get some money? If so, from whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After several months, I looked up Mr. -- the chief, Mr. Ivica Santic. Of course, he had sent these troops there to the mountain lodge, Zabrdze, and he said that they would compensate me, but at one point, he gave me a one-time assistance, around 70 German marks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that in some currency other than German marks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. These were not German marks. They were Bosnian dinars. At that time, they were also known as the red coupons. But the value was 70 German marks, the equivalence of 70 German marks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do as Cerkez instructed and leave the lodge, returning to your then home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that in --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I asked -- yes, it was in the apartment blocks. I said, "What should I use to -- how am I going to get back there? Is there a truck going back to Vitez?" And he said that the registration plate was KZ. The driver was very nice to me, and he took me and my son, because I was up there with him, he brought me home, and after that, I had no further business and contact with that facility, and I don't know what happened there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's not necessary or right for you to identify yourself, even by your address, so be careful in the answers you give, but is it right that your home at that stage was a flat in a block of flats which was effectively on the main road from Vitez to Busovaca, somewhere within Dubravica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Donja Dubravica, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having lost your employment in April 1992, can you remember the precise date in April that Cerkez called?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that that was April 3rd, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, between then and March of 1993, have any other job or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I had lost my job, as did my two sons. Because I had envisaged employing both of my sons there because this was my livelihood, my sons were unemployed, and I wanted them to work there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dealing with that same period, April 1992 to March 1993, which leading figures, leading local figures did you see on the television from time to time? First of all, did you ever see anything of Cerkez himself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. With a group of people who held press conferences, who held meetings, these were open conferences which were broadcast on television, that is, certain reports were on television, but I did not see a direct proceedings, a live proceedings. But I saw when they had -- well, when they held the joint meetings with the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the Croat leaders that you saw on the television from time to time in that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were several of them. I know quite well Anto Valenta and Pero Skopljak, Ivica Santic and Mario Cerkez, Blaskic, and there were an additional two whose names I forgot. I don't know now. I forgot their names. They left the area soon thereafter; I don't know where they went, but I saw them there. But until the 15th of April, 1993, that is, on that last evening, on the 15th of April, at 7.10, that they had a meeting, I don't know with whom, and they said that there was no agreement with Muslims --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you there in order that we can deal with things in chronological order. Did you at this time know by sight or in any other way the man Dario Kordic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I knew him from television. I had no direct contact. Perhaps I saw him two or three times maybe in front of the restaurant in Kruscica, from a distance of about 20 to 30 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to come to those sightings in a few minutes, but before I do, to keep in chronological order, paragraph 10, was a man called Samir Trako killed on a day in May 1992? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How soon after his death did you learn of the death?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Somebody called up my brother on the telephone and told him, and sometime later people from the Territorial Defence came and said that Samir had been killed in the hotel that night.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the physical condition of these two men when you saw them a few days after the apparent killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in a very difficult situation. They had to go to hospital. I don't know how long they stayed in hospital, but they had to be hospitalised for them to have a medical examination, because they were beaten up, their bodies were all black and blue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just "Yes" or "No" to this question. Did either of these men claim to have been an eyewitness to the killing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which one, or was it both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both of them went out together. They were taken out of the basement after the torture and they went out on the stairs, and Samir was killed at that particular point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Which one of these told you what had happened or was it both of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Both of them, both of them told me, but Senad Petak more because I was with him more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell us, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just before you get that far, this is going to be the repetition of what somebody told somebody else, one of whom is potentially coming here?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. As we're not in private session, we must speak carefully about that, but nothing is known, of course, for certain about witness availability. As to this topic, its admissibility has been ruled on earlier, and at that earlier stage, evidence was given from a witness of what he was told of the circumstances. This evidence comes directly from the mouth of an eyewitness. As with all evidence of this quality, its value is, in our respectful submission -- or its evaluation is for later, but it would, in our respectful submission, be quite wrong to think of excluding it at this stage, and it would be appropriate to hear from the witness, what she has been told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Eyewitness through this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you tell us, please, what you were told by Senad Petak of what had happened in relation to Samir Trako?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please. I'm so sorry, I wasn't looking at you. Very rude of me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of what was said, and it was the topic of the day at that particular moment, everybody asked, "Do you know?" Well, when they were taken out, Suad Trako and (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who killed him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that particular moment, quite simply that's what we heard, it was said that that man killed him. What's his name? He was also from Kruscica. I knew his surname, but I've forgotten it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But what did --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But afterwards, when he was taken into custody and taken away, he was taken to prison, he made a statement -- not to me, but that's what people said -- that he said, "I didn't kill Trako, but you'll hear who did."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, now we are dealing with different hearsay, I think. I object to such question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's try and get what the point is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He -- as he saw that just Cerkez was there and that other young man, however, he assessed that Cerkez killed Samir.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the other man you've been speaking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's try and clear this up. Can you help us, please, Witness R?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is -- it was his idea, his thought. He thought that it was correct, and, well, I don't know, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) and not that other young man. Vukadinovic was his name. It's come to me now, that Vukadinovic had not shot Samir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The evidence has been given. What weight we give to it is entirely a matter for us, if any.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Correct. Your Honours, I just wanted to notice, since you mentioned that perhaps the translation was not correct, I would like to assure you that it was very precise and correct, because I was following both English and Croatian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness R, did Suad Trako say anything about the events that had happened? Did he give an account of how Samir Trako had been killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Suad?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Suad was also so beaten up that he couldn't even see out of his eyes. His face was all massacred and, quite simply, he wasn't able to see where he was going or what he was looking at. That was the state he was in. He was so beaten up and massacred, his face and his eyes were all swollen and he couldn't even think about it when he went out. But he had such a great -- had put forth such a great deal of effort to look at Samir when Samir lay there, lay down there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. These two, did they tell you what had happened to them after the killing of Trako, Samir Trako, and before they returned to the area where you were living, or wherever it was that you met them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, based on stories told, people came to the house to see what had happened and they told their story, that they were in the beer-drinking place, that they were captured by some people in this beer-drinking place, and they were beaten up. And afterwards, when they were taken out, that's what they said, they were taken to Kruscica by some sort of car to the forest up there or wood, and from the cave they had bags on their faces and they were thrown down there from the cave, so that the Croats thought they were already dead. However, other people turned up, or these people came back to see what had happened to them. They had come to, they had regained consciousness, and they were taken somewhere. I don't know where, but they were imprisoned two days after that and nobody knew what had happened to them. However, with the assistance of their relatives, they were found, and they were brought back in the state of health that they were in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness R, I'm now going to turn to other events that you saw, between April '92 and March '93, from your flat or in the area of your flat. Was there, near to your flat, a coffee house called Kruscica which had once belonged to a Muslim named Faruk Zukic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he lose his possession or occupation of that coffee house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that coffee house taken from him, and if so, by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was taken away from him, because at the time Vlado Krizanac, called Willy [as interpreted], was the boss. He was the main one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say he was the boss, was he a Muslim, or Croat, or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His brothers' first names were, please? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was Stjepan and there was -- I've forgotten, but there were three brothers, and this particular one, Vlado, was the head person in this Kruscica coffee house where meetings were held. All the army went in there, the HVO and the Jokers, as they were called. They would drink there, and HOS at the beginning too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a view from your flat or from the area around your flat of the inside of the coffee house or only of the garden and the entrance area to the coffee house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had a table and chairs, and we sat there all the time throughout the day, and this was 20 metres away from our table to the Kruscica coffee house. We could see everything because there was just a small hedge between the coffee house and our yard, where we sat. And so we could see everything. We could see the comings and goings. Personally, we could recognise the people who came and went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of that period of time, '92 to '93, did you see anything of any leading figures at or near the coffee house? First Blaskic, did you see him at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once or more than once?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps twice I saw him; once by a car -- Andrija Livancic was seeing to his tyre. We were sitting -- a group of women were sitting in the yard. And another time he came in front of the coffee house. He talked to Vlado and then left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It should be explained that there's a tyre repair garage nearby as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the same yard, the coffee house and the tyre repair shop. It was a premises for both these establishments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already told us that Kordic was there a few times. When he arrived, what did he do? Did he go into the coffee house or did he stay outside?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By an old apple tree, I saw him standing there once, and he was talking to Vlado about something, and there was some other men there too. And on one occasion, he went inside and came out quickly again. I don't know why he went inside, whether to get some information or a drink, I don't know, but that is where the information service, so to speak, was where they discussed things and everything, in the coffee house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the coffee house some distance back from the main road, reached by a little lane or road of its own?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. It was a broad area from the road towards the facility. There was a large parking space, perhaps 15 to 20 metres. Not more than that, though. That was the distance from the road to the facility. It was a parking space.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Staying with Dario Kordic, paragraph 21, was there an incident involving a soldier called Nuk, son of Nikola, that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. There were a lot of people out on the road for security purposes, and we were standing around by the kiosk next to the road, and Nuk, son of Nikola, I don't know his name, I know his father's name, he was armed, he had a helmet and flack jacket, and there were a lot of troops there, and they didn't let any civilians stand there next to the kiosk. And when we asked -- when people asked why they were doing this, he said, "The main person is passing, Kordic is passing, and nobody must be present, nobody must be here, because he has to pass by calmly and safely." And I left, my husband stayed on, and he said, "There's no reason, I'm not armed." Well Nuk said, "You better clear off or I'll shoot." And my husband went home. He was terribly pale and frightened because this man had already cocked his rifle at him and said that if he didn't leave, he would shoot. And, of course, my husband just turned around and went home. There's about 20 metres from the road to my home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see anything of Kordic passing by, if he did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. We couldn't see because we were made to go back into the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that the only time you were aware of Kordic apparently passing on the main road, or was there any other occasion or occasions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. He passed by twice with all the security around. I was at my brother's in Novaci, and some of the army was there. Some were standing about, others were sitting down in a sort of a trench, and one of the men said to me, "Hurry up, go home, because no passage is allowed here because Colonel Kordic is about to pass by from Busovaca to Vitez."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you ever aware of in whose company he may be travelling or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Well, yes, he was escorted by the HVO, if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Returning to named people who visited this coffee house, did you know the name or the man Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. A terrible name for us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he use that coffee house? If so, with what frequency, and how was he addressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. Of course. Yes. He always wore black, a black uniform, and his soldiers wore black uniforms too, and it said Jokeri on it, the Jokers, and they had a great metal "U" insignia, and it said Vitezovi on the other. So Vitezovi, and Jokeri, with a skull emblem on the sleeve, and others had this skull sign on their backs, depending on the kind of uniform they were wearing. But they had black shirts, black trousers -- everything was black; it all looked terrible -- black caps, and they had this emblem, the "U" sign on their caps, and they said that they were proud to be Ustashas, that they were the army of Pavelic, and that they were accepted by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next name I want you to deal with is Jozo Buha.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about him? Was he in the area? Did he use the cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, every day. Jozo Buha, a year prior to that, from 1991 perhaps, he would make lists of the Muslim inhabitants. If the number would change, the number of Muslims, he would draw up a new list to know who was where, and when I asked him why he did that, he said, "Well, for security reasons, for evacuation, if the Chetniks, for example, attacked," and I said -- well, first of all, he made a list of Croats for Croatia, and then he said, "Well, I'm going to write your name down too," and I said, "Well, my name is not down on the list," and he said, "Well, it's not necessary because we know you." So quite simply, he would draw up this list with information of where the Muslims lived because it was easy to reach the Muslim houses. Jozo Buha did this on behalf of the local community of Donja Dubravica, and he was very proud to say that it was Pavelic's army, that they would be victorious, that they would win over the Muslims, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's turn to the 15th of April of 1993. You'd already started to tell us, I think, about a television broadcast. Just explain what it was you saw.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it was like this: I went to my brother's house, my brothers were there and my relations, the people that come from my native village, and I went to them on the eve --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't identify the village by name. It's in the summary of your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. The village has 150 houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, it's a matter for you, but you don't have to name it. You went to your brother's house --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My brother came from the market, it was growing dusk, and he said, "The Muslims are being arrested and taken away to some facilities, to schools, I don't know where else," and I said, "Well, do I dare go home?" He said, "Well, I don't advise it. It would be better for you to stay." So I called my husband up and asked him what the situation was like, whether he was able to see anything. He said, "I can see nothing. I'm in the house," and I said, "Well, my brother told me that Muslims were being taken away, group by group. Some had been taken to the school in Donja Dubravica." However, at 7.00 and 10.00 in the evening, there was the Croatian news, and at the beginning, Mr. Kordic said the following, he said: "We negotiated with the Muslims and we're not going to do that anymore because there can be no more negotiations with them. We are declaring war and we have to fight a war with them." Those were the words of Mr. Kordic, if I can say "mister" for him. And --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything else that Kordic said in the television interview that you want to tell us about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The news bulletin lasted for only ten minutes. It was between 7.00 and 7.10 p.m. I don't know what -- why, we asked ourselves why? Why a war with the Muslims? We didn't know why. We weren't armed; we had no weapons; we didn't even think of a war for the Croats to declare war with us. We were surprised because we were up there on the line together fighting another enemy. However, that's what they said. In the morning, at 6.30, I stayed with my brother, I wasn't able to go, but the next morning, at 6.30, I was woken up by the shell. I went downstairs; I woke the others up. This was at 5.30 in the morning, 5.30, and it was the beginning of the shooting at that place where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Taking this comparatively shortly, and I shall lead, unless I'm invited not to, from paragraph 28, did you, with about 180 villagers, find yourself rounded up by HVO soldiers, some of whom you could recognise, indeed, some of them being the brothers Miro Kulic and Zoran Kulic and Miro Karin from Rijeka? You can just say yes to that if that's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kulic, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taken to a shelter where you had to sleep on a concrete floor, but you weren't otherwise maltreated at that stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that time, we weren't mistreated because it was the beginning. We hid. But when they came in two days later, that was the 18th, and when they went to the settlement, they put us up -- they quite simply said that we had to go to that shelter. The house was -- well, yes, it's not important. It was a shelter; it doesn't matter who it belonged to. However, we were there on the concrete floor, of course, because the house was under construction. It hadn't been completed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to cut you short in order to save time and, I hope, make it easy for you to go back swiftly home. On the 19th of April, did Kulic, Miro Kulic, come to the shelter, saying that he had orders from his commander, Karlo Grabovac, to pick up the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but to call the people and to make a list of them, of all the inhabitants living there, so that they had the exact number of people, so that they knew how many of us lived there, and Ekrem had to do this. That man was named Ekrem; he had to do that. He had to draw up a list of all of us. The list was handed over and we went back to the shelter. The next morning, one again, Miro Kulic came to fetch us. He had been given orders from Karlo Grabovac to take us there because he had received orders from Kraljevic, Darko Kraljevic, to take us all to the Perina Caira field. Do you want me to continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we went out. We complained and asked why we were being taken there, but there was nothing to be done. Miro went first, carrying a white flag in front of us. We all went in a group, nobody dared not go, and when we got to the exit of the settlement, towards the automobile association and the Dubravica elementary school, Jozo Buha shot at us from a hill, those who were in the column. Luckily, he didn't hit anybody. Miro just shouted, "Jozo, don't shoot. I'm with them and don't shoot. They have to go to the destination" he had been told. He took us to the meadow and we waited and waited there, and Kraljevic came up, Darko Kraljevic got there later on with another five -- allegedly, they were killers and had to finish the job. However --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the men separated from the women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first group of seven men had already been singled out, and they said this was for a beginning, for liquidation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was one of those men a doctor? Was his bag taken and thrown into a ditch or a stream?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You see, yes, there was a doctor, a surgeon, Trako Mujic, who was also lined up, and he addressed Kraljevic and he said, "These people need me." He said, "Nobody will need you." He grabbed his bag and said he wouldn't need it anymore, and all those things were thrown into the Lasva River, and they flowed down the Lasva. He gave a sign for all of those who were there to get ready to finish off this group of seven. When he had lined them up, he said, "Now you will see what Ustashas can do." He took my brother by his shirt collar and said, "You will pay in particular." Nobody said a word, they were all silent, and then before they got ready to do it, two UNPROFOR personnel carriers stopped just there at the edge of the meadow, and they saw us there. When Kraljevic saw UNPROFOR, he said that he would go and tell them to get lost because nobody must see what was going to happen except us. So Karlo Grabovac went to warn them, to tell them to go away, that they mustn't take any photographs because this was something they mustn't know. However, we thank one person, and I will never say that name in public, because they called UNPROFOR to come and save those 180 victims, and I have every respect for that person. Then Kraljevic said, "We won't kill you here. Take them to the school," and he took these two men, escorted them to the school. They stayed at the school. We remained waiting, and then suddenly they ordered us to go back home. We went back to our settlement. One-hundred and eighty of us had to be put up in two houses; of course, there wasn't room enough, but we had to make due, whereas our houses that were left without anyone inside were looted, and when we got back, everything was upside down, ransacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we leave that event, did Kraljevic make clear how many people were to be executed, if more than that first seven, or did he not make that clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The plan was for us all to be executed, all of us who were there, all the inhabitants of that settlement, because he was ready to liquidate all of us who were there. That was Darko Kraljevic's intention, to do it. Who gave the orders and whose idea it was, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The people who were there, were they all Muslims, in your group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were detained following this incident, and we know that the men, the seven men returned as well. Was there an occasion when soldiers, paragraph 44, came back to the village and made inquiries of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A small group of people who were some sort of supervisors, guards, apparently, to protect us, so that nobody would kidnap us or take us away; however, sometimes they were there, sometimes they were not, but they didn't even fear that we would go anywhere because we didn't have anywhere to go. Nobody came, UNPROFOR or the Red Cross or anyone, to identify us over a period of 21 days. Once UNPROFOR headed towards us, they reached as far as the bridge, they were shot at, they went back, and we were never registered. Then once the municipal Red Cross came. We thought they had come to register us. We thought this list was being made so they would know where we were, but the list was being made for another purpose. The municipal Red Cross, which was under the HVO, didn't ask us anything. They just saw that we were there, turned around, and went back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did HVO soldiers ever search the houses in which you were staying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you, they searched all the houses and took with them whatever they wanted. They weren't real soldiers. They were thugs who were looting other people's houses. Those who were guarding us, they didn't provoke us in any sense. There was a young man of 16 who cried, and he said, "Why aren't I going to school? I want to live. I don't want to watch guard over you." He was a Croat, a soldier of 16.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) and what they had intended to happen did not happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to move on, again to save you time, to paragraphs 45 to 48. Just yes or no to this, because it may not particularly concern the Tribunal, this Tribunal, just yes or no: Were you aware of some rapes or alleged rapes at about this time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just yes or no to this: Was the man Bralo said to have been involved in one rape? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just yes or no to this: Did you hear something of what Bralo had said about the rape he was alleged to have committed? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't hear Bralo say this, but women told me who had been passing by the window that they heard him say, "This was worse for me --"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Pause there. I'm sorry. So it was women who were passing the window who heard what it was Bralo had said; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, women who were inside, but Bralo was passing by the window with a number of soldiers, and he said that this had been worse for him than to kill 50 people in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you detained in your village until the 7th of May, when you were released, thanks to negotiations between a Muslim doctor and a Croat doctor, Bruno Buzuk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then walk to Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Accompanied by 11 people who stayed in your village, including two brothers who you've named in your statement and summary and who were later killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Eleven of them stayed behind. UNPROFOR came to us, to Gornja Dubravica, and asked whether any citizen had stayed behind. We said, "Yes, 11 of them." They went to pick them up, to bring them over too. However, they didn't want to come. Only the wife of one of these men came because she was disabled and she couldn't go on foot. The others stayed, and in about a month and a half later, they too had to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, I should like to learn from the witness what is the distance between the village and Zenica which she had to cover on foot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Via Vjetrenica, it is 18 kilometres, and if you take the roundabout route, it is 23 kilometres. We went across Vjetrenica, Mount Vjetrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope that satisfies the Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One other question of geography that I was going to ask you. Approximately how far east of the boundaries of Vitez was your community in terms of metres or kilometres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From which spot do you mean? From what town?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our municipality is in Vitez, but where I lived, it may be a kilometre and 200, 300 metres from the actual municipality building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Returning to the events following your walk to Zenica, I think you may have confirmed, and I just want to check this, that the two brothers, I can perhaps give their last name or both their names, Siljak, they were killed, were they? They stayed behind and they were killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Their throats were slit. They weren't killed. They were slaughtered. Apparently, they played ball with their heads. That was the story. I wasn't there, but people said, "Whose heads are they?" In any event, to this day, they have no grave, and nobody knows where their bodies are.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think your husband had been kept meanwhile in Dubravica school.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to confirm that your son, who had been a policeman, was, as you understood it, detained in the SDK building until the 5th of May --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- released and rearrested, taken with other prisoners to Kaonik, killed on the 20th of June --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- and his body recovered from the Lasva River, close to Kaonik, on the 23rd of June?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, and he's buried in Busovaca seven days later. Then the demand was made for the bodies of five of them to be exhumed for the purposes of exchange, and my son was exchanged. The funeral was on the 19th of July. My son was executed. You could see from his documents, which had holes in them. I don't know about the others. When he was exchanged, he was cut up in pieces as if they were pieces of meat. They practised massacring on his dead body.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I produce through the witness two exhibits, Z1751 and Z2210,8? Each must be under seal because of anonymity. The first is a diagram that shows, very schematically, the block of flats and the coffee house, and the second is the death certificate of her son. But they don't have to be shown publicly, and they won't take any time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness R, is the first exhibit that I've shown you just the diagram that you drew, at the time that you were making one of your statements, that shows the block of flats and the coffee house, and is the second exhibit the death certificate of your son, but you notice that the place of his death is recorded there as "Lasva-Zenica", fourth line down, which is inaccurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The killing was done between Lasva and Zenica, at Kaonik. Actually, between Busovaca and Lasva, not Zenica. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Two other questions and then I'm finished. Paragraphs 32 and 33, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him doing anything in the course of these events you've told us about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was some sort of a commander of that group, the group that was there that acted as guards, sentries, I don't know what. He was the one in charge, he was the one they obeyed, and I don't know who gave him his orders. In any event, they asked Karlo about everything. Whatever he said, they had to do. Karlo Grabovac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: His father's name was what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Jozo, a nice man who used to work in the post office. He was retired. He was head of the post office. This is his son. He has only one son, and that son is Karlo. He worked in the Impregnacija factory with my husband, where my husband also worked. We know each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine, I think. One matter of detail that may be a detail for you to correct and deal with or it may be for the transcript, but you told us earlier about Vlado Krizanac and, indeed, about his brothers; paragraph 14. What was the nickname for Vlado?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sidi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I think in the transcript, it's "Willy", and it's Sidi?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sidi.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those are the only questions I ask.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's how everyone called him. And Willy was the nickname of Marko Stipinovic, a good organiser of crimes too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. That would be a suitable time to adjourn. Who is going to cross-examine now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Cerkez Defence will go first, with your permission, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, obviously it would be desirable, if it's possible, to finish this witness today. There will be an hour remaining once we come back. No doubt you'll make every effort.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Certainly, I will, Sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 4.00, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I apologise, because I have to address you with your pseudonym, as Witness R, rather than your name, and I should like to take advantage of this opportunity to express my condolences because of the loss of your son. I should like to ask you, in the interest of expediency, to answer a few introductory questions. What education do you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Elementary school education.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Nothing more than that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you later acquire any vocational training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What was your source of living?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My husband's salary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You were not employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You told us that you were in this mountain lodge when Cerkez came with some soldiers. Is it true that this mountain lodge was called Jovica Kosanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It is on a mountain above Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think the distance is about 12 kilometres from the village of Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, because I never measured the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But we can agree that it is not very close to Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it is an area where, in addition to the mountain lodge, there were quite a number of weekend homes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but on the other side, not nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you say "not nearby" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mean not close to the mountain lodge. It was maybe 200 metres, 500 metres, or maybe a whole kilometre from the nearest weekend home, so 500 metres away was the area where these holiday homes were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you own anything in that mountain lodge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You had a contract on a lease, you had a lease? Who did you sign this contract with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With the Mountaineering Society of Vitez, Latif Barucija, Fahra Sivro. But, in any event, with two men who were responsible for this mountain lodge, and I signed a contract with them as caretaker.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When Cerkez came with those soldiers, according to what you told us -- in fact, you said he addressed you as madam -- was he polite with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The soldiers and Cerkez were armed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Please, don't repeat what I'm saying. Allow me to put the questions to you. So they were armed. Is it normal for soldiers to be armed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's not a question you need answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did any of those soldiers threaten with his weapon, point his weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Madam, this happened on the 3rd of April, 1992. At that time, in Vitez and the surroundings, there were no inter-ethnic conflicts at the time; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But at that time already, the aggression had started by the JNA against Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At the time, military conscripts, both Muslims and Croats, or Bosniaks, as some people prefer to be called, that is, the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims, went to the battlefront in the republic to fight the JNA; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And these soldiers that came with Cerkez, as far as you understood, were part of that army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but they were not a mixed army. They were a single ethnic army. They were the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, but from the conversation, you were able to gather that they were preparing to go to the front line to fight the aggressor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what they said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At the time, did you hear that in April 1992, the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina had declared a state of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of course. I don't know really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that there was a mobilisation period, where men were being called up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let us go back for a moment to those weekend houses. In view of the fact that you were in touch with the mountain lodge, there were frequent instances of burglaries of those weekend homes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I saw weekend homes destroyed and others looted because we would pass by them sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: These HVO soldiers who came with Cerkez and captured the area, did you hear from them, that they would try to protect the property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You told us today that after being told to contact the municipality for compensation, you received in Bosnian coupons the equivalence of 70 marks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you gave two previous statements to the investigators. So you agree that you made a statement in August 1996, a detailed one, and another one in September 1998, slightly shorter. In that statement, the first one from 1996, you said, with reference to that event, that about a month later, through the SDK service, you received an amount equivalent to 700 German marks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But that is what it says in the statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's a mistake. That's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your statement from 1998, you said that you received 70 German marks, but you did not mention the SDK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is what I got through the SDK, and this can be verified to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So it is true that you got the money from the SDK?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And that's all I got.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So through the SDK, you didn't receive 700, but 70 marks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This money that you got, did it correspond to the income you had lost?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No where near that. The value was much greater. My effort, the cleaning I had done, my supplies, these were all goods that I had signed up for. I was responsible for them. The value would be much greater in peacetime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you still hadn't started working there. You had just prepared it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I had already started working. I had already taken in guests.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm still not quite clear about your answers in connection with Mario Cerkez's appearance on television, so I have only one question for you, and that is: Did you ever see Cerkez on television in the company of Valenta?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, several times. Valenta was there almost regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Are you sure that it wasn't General Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes the whole group was there, all of them. When they had press conferences or meetings that were public and that were shown on television, Valenta was almost always there because he was the person most responsible for the ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't come to my place. I went to see them. They are my relatives. I went to visit them. They were brought in three days later because nobody knew where they were hidden. It was upon the insistence of the family that they were brought back in a very bad condition. They could hardly talk. At that time, they didn't really want to see anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, you told us all that. But tell us, please, did you learn then that after that unfortunate event, they went to the hotel, to the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that they had been in Zenica at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Allegedly, they spent seven days there. I don't know whether it was seven days, but they were in hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How then could they see you on the third day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you. They were brought back home, and from their home, they were taken to hospital because they needed medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you saw them before they went to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as soon as they were brought back, that morning, I was there. I went to see how they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And they didn't mention then that they were in the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They just mentioned that they were in the restaurant, in the pub in the cellar of the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But afterward, did they mention that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that. Just a moment, please. Correction. It was said they had been brought from the police that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When they came home, they were brought from the police. That is what they said, so that is their story.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Witness R, in the statement you gave to the investigators in September 1998, I would like to quote a sentence, an excerpt of what you said then. You said: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I interrupt, but I wonder whether Mr. Kovacic will recall the care that's got to be taken with this witness, if he is going to read passages out that identify. Obviously, the process of redaction can go on, but it's, I gather, already been difficult for the staff. Perhaps he can be more careful. We've had this problem before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I was trying to be very careful and slow. I could repeat it, if you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not the repetition. It's anything which might lead to identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. But both those persons have many relatives. They are a big family.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Does this mean that either of these two could have told you that they saw the actual murder or that they had heard about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means that at that point, when they were brought out of this beer cellar, that they went to the -- that there at the hotel, there was only Cerkez and -- again, I forget his name --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean Vukadinovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Vukadinovic. However, they saw that Samir was killed. Samir fell down as they were coming out to this plateau, that is when Samir fell, but apparently Vukadinovic had killed him, but then this same Vukadinovic, I don't know whom he told this to, but he said that he didn't do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. We have heard that. So did they tell you that the guests who were in that beer cellar came out running to the lobby of the hotel, including Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not what they told me. That is not what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So they said that they were not down in the beer cellar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were there in the beer cellar, and then they were brought out and beaten up. So when they were brought up, Samir was killed, and then they just know that this Vukadinovic said that he did not kill Samir. And I would like this to end, that this question be the last one so that I don't repeat myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Madam, were they physically attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were they beaten up down in the beer cellar before the murder took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. And then they were again beaten up after the murder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know about that. They were taken to the woods in Kruscica and they were thrown down some rocks, and all this happened in the same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you hear whether they received some medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. Whether that was in the health centre in Vitez or somewhere else, I don't know, but they came back with casts around their necks, bandaged, and they practically couldn't move.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, I think you may be upsetting the witness by this line of questioning. Now, if there's anything you particularly want to ask about Mr. Cerkez, I think we've had all the detail on this particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you allow me, I'm just on the last question connected to this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, but then I suggest you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You told us, and if you would just confirm this to us by just saying yes or no, whether this is correct or not, you told us that Senad had a judgement on who shot the deceased.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because there were only the two of them there, Cerkez and Vukadinovic, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Madam, you said that Vukadinovic was in prison in Split.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were told that he was taken there for his own safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that he was in prison.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the story that was circulated widely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Madam, is it correct that one of these two nephews, that is, one of the two persons we have mentioned, I am not going to mention the names, that he was in a juvenile corrections centre as a juvenile?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who are you referring to? If you're mentioning names, you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Just one more thing. In May 1992, at the time when this murder took place, regarding the situation in April, there was no persecution, there was no conflict between the Muslims and the Croats, and still there was an ongoing aggression of the Serbs against the Bosniaks; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In part of your statement, you mentioned this cafe which you said the HVO -- you said some persons, apparently referring to the HVO, the Cafe Zukic, that it was forcibly taken away from this man?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And since this was your immediate neighbourhood, do you know whether the municipality compensated the man for the requisitioned facility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only know he invested a lot of money in there. I don't know whether he had really started working there. But it was at this time that this property was taken away from him, and I know that he -- from last I saw him, he still was not compensated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But do you know whether this was an organised unit who took it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that somebody had asked that it should be taken away from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But he didn't say who it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but can I just answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor will ask you additional questions, and then you may offer an answer. Madam, you also mentioned Darko Kraljevic. You said that he was a Joker. In your previous statements, you expressly stated that he was a Joker, and now you say that the Jokers and Vitezovi were one and the same, that all their badges were worn together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were worn together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Madam, are you sure that Darko Kraljevic and his members were calling themselves Jokers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was the chief of them. Jokers and Vitezovi, this is what they were called. They were called Kraljevic's Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Madam, if you could just answer very simply, do you know that -- are you sure that Kraljevic was commander of the Jokers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, what turns --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It is impeachment, Your Honour. The witness is claiming that she doesn't know exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have the point in mind, that you say there's other evidence that Kraljevic was the leader of the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then I have no --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have the point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Madam, when you testified about the horrible experiences you had when you were detained, you said that you would not disclose names but that you were grateful to the person who called UNPROFOR up. I'm not asking for a name, but was it a Croat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be a Croat or Croatian man or woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was this person wearing an HVO uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could we agree, which would follow from your statement, but you did not state it expressly so I need to ask you, at the time when you were in Dubravica, in the school, when your husband was there and you were in the neighbourhood, Darko Kraljevic's troops were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All different troops who wanted to torture and mistreat detainees paraded through the school in Dubravica, not only the Vitezovi and the Jokers and the HOS. Anybody who wanted to torture the detainees came through this school building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Madam, when you say "HVO", do you refer to all the troops which were on the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Every troop had insignia. I don't know whether all the HOS went to the HVO. Jokers, I don't think, were the HVO, per se. They had -- they were an independent unit. But the HVO was the head of all the troops who were in Vitez. If they were not, why didn't they prevent this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is this what you know directly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know this from all the stories that went around.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. You said that Kraljevic's plan was to kill you all, and you meant -- I guess you were referring to everybody in Donja Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all of us civilians who were in Dubravica, in -- not in the school building, he had ordered that we were all to be taken out to the open field, and this was to be done I don't know by whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Madam, did you see this plan? Did you hear about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I witnessed it. I was just there and waiting when we would be lined up. I'm not excited. This is just the way I speak. We were all waiting to see when our turn would come.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you never saw this in writing, nor did anybody tell you that this was the plan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know that I can answer with "Yes" or "No", but I can tell you specifically that there was a plan. A plan existed that we should all be done away with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Eventually, of the group that you said Darko Kraljevic separated in order to have them killed, you said that fortunately UNPROFOR came and they were all released, nobody was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true, nobody was killed, and that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Madam, you also mention in your statement that your husband suffered a heart attack because he was a heart patient?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the war, he had two heart attacks, and he was pronounced clinically dead by doctors in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And the HVO transferred him to the health centre in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and then the UNPROFOR took it over from there. They said that they took over the body and they brought him to Travnik and just dumped him at the hospital in Travnik without ever providing any information. And only when he was -- the third day after he was considered dead, he woke up on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Madam, you said that at one point, the HVO soldiers came to Donja Dubravica and you complained and asked for protection, to be protected from Darko Kraljevic's men. Do you agree that, in a way, they did attempt to protect you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Those to whom you complained, whose protection you asked.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can respond to this very specifically. The HVO had control over this area for 20 days. We were a few neighbours and we had no problems, and they protected us so that nobody would come from Jozo Buha's group from over the hill, so they protected us. Secondly, the Jokers came the night before we were driven out of this neighbourhood. That's when they raped these women, and we couldn't ask for protection of them because we wouldn't -- we didn't have anyone to ask it from. They wouldn't have given it to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness R, did you ever hear with whom Bralo was with, Cicko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was with Vitezovi or Jokers. To us, it was the same. Vitezovi and Jokers were one and the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Madam, my apologies to you, and I'm not going to ask you about this tragic incident, murder.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ask anything you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that his body was found between Lasva and Busovaca. That is outside of the Vitez municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Madam, I have only one additional question for you. When you started on the way to Zenica on the mountain road through Vrhovine and Poculica, you said how many kilometres that is, the distance, and beyond Poculica, the territories under the ABiH are controlled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, actually beyond Dubravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So Dubravica was the line of separation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So did you ask of the -- why didn't you ask of ABiH army to give you a lift?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me be allowed to tell you this. We came to Dubravica on foot, and then individuals from Zenica, and some people of goodwill, they all came in their private vehicles, on buses, they drove, they came to save us. Some walked on foot. Some got lifts from -- got lifts in different vehicles, but everybody wanted to leave as soon as possible. A friend of mine came from Zenica, so he took me in his vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you only all were walking to Poculica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I don't know how long it was; two, three kilometres. But there was sniper fire from the Krizancevo Gaj, and all this was controlled all the way until Poculica. This whole area was under their control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, madam. This is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Madam, now let me introduce myself. I am a lawyer from Zagreb, Mitko Naumovski, and I'm one of the Defence counsel for Mr. Drago Kordic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm happy to know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask you a few very brief questions on one single topic. On the 15th of April, 1993, from 7.00, you watched television at your brother's house, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We watched -- we did not watch Croatian -- the Croatian programme but we switched over to the Bosnian television programme.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Madam, I just took note of the fact that you were watching television. I didn't say what you were watching.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were watching television. I watched television, and we watched up until --

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Please, madam, may I proceed with my questioning? What you saw on television was a press conference, in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: At that press conference, there were a number of individuals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, five or six people. They were sitting in the television studio, in a hall. I don't know where. Anyway, that's what it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wanted to clarify one point, that it was in fact a press conference, and that press conference, on the 15th of October, 1993, the Court has already had occasion to hear about, and part of it was shown here, part of that press conference, and the transcript has also been tendered into evidence, and so I'm sure that Your Honours will be able to see exactly what Mr. Kordic said on the occasion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's challenged, is it, that he said that there would be no more negotiations and that the Croats would be fighting a war? Is that in dispute?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Anything else you want to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence of Mr. Kordic sometimes has a little more questions to ask, and we consider that that is necessary for protecting the interests of our client, Mr. Kordic. But in this instance, we're going to reduce time and be brief, and so we have no more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would like you to have more questions and then I could answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I just add that we don't consider it essential, but as the witness said so, let me say that Mr. Kordic was never on the particular premises that she mentioned that he was, but we don't think it's important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that what I said was quite certain but if you say so, perhaps you were there, so you know better than me. I then apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Naumovski. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a few points.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How was Mr. Kordic dressed when he was at the cafe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was dressed in a camouflage uniform with a cap and a chequerboard emblem on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The second point, you have been asked questions about the plan to kill the people in the meadow. One matter of detail you can help us with. It's paragraphs 38 and 39. While the seven men had been separated, was there a vehicle present with some kind of gun on it or some kind of armament on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a big truck on the bridge, at the entrance to the bridge, and on it was a sort of mortar, a long barrel, which was aimed at the direction of the settlement where we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was in charge of that vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Karlo Grabovac was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so that vehicle was aiming in the direction of whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the village, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I would like to object on the basis that those issues were not even touched during the cross, so it is indeed a continuation of direct. It is not redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There was an issue, I recollect, as to whether there was a plan to kill the people in the field, so any evidence relevant to that must be admissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'll just deal with paragraph 39, but of course we notice that there has been no challenge by the Defence in relation to the involvement of Karlo Grabovac on 31 and onwards, but if Mr. Kovacic wants to challenge 38 and 39, I would personally have no objection to his being allowed to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, let's not take more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This truck that you saw, had it been used on any earlier occasions, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, probably. That mortar, which was parked up on the bridge, that was, in fact, the blockade of the bridge, and perhaps from that particular mortar they fired at the settlement in which we lived, because from all sides, from all weapons, this settlement where we lived was attacked. Luckily, not too many of us died.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The same objection. The mortar was not even mentioned.
