utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nice, is there anything more you want?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, two other questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of course, all the groups came there, the army, the Jokers, the civilians. Everything was there, and it was a real organisation for agreement, for information, and that was the main sort of -- where all the main events took place, in that particular coffee house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know what explanation, if any, was given to the occupier when he was forced out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: An explanation was given, and I was told this by this individual. He asked that they pay compensation, and they threatened to kill him, that he shouldn't come there anymore, and after the war it would be his again. So those were the words he used to tell me about that event, as you asked me that particular question, I know what he said when we talked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Then the last question on a similar topic but relating to your lodge. How near or far was your lodge from the Serb front line, if you can help us, at the time that the lodge was taken from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very far away, very far. It wasn't -- there weren't any Serbs on one side or the other or the third. They weren't in the vicinity. There were no Serbs there in the vicinity. There was Vlasic. That's a long way off. There was the Karaula Travnik, there was Donji Vakuf and so on. But in the vicinity, there was no Serbian army or front line with the Serbs, against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, was anything said about the use that would be put of your lodge or did you discover what use your lodge was put to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was informed -- I've already answered that question. I think I've already answered why my particular mountain lodge was taken away from me, where I was to have worked, and this incurred thousands of marks in damages because I wasn't able to work it further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: May I just briefly pose -- the question implies that the witness was the owner of the object, which the witness really said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not terribly important. I think it's clear that she wasn't. She ran a business there, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But what use was the lodge put to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it rendered a service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When it was taken over by the HVO, what use did they put it to; do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly what use, because I left the same day. You know why they came. I was told -- Cerkez told me, when I asked him, "What am I to do now and what does all this mean," and he told me, "You're asking too much. You'll learn in due course."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Nothing else, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness R, thank you very much for coming to the International Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you for inviting me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That concludes your evidence. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may, please, may I just tell the public a detail, tell them of a detail?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, very briefly, if you must.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I present something? It's very brief. This piece of paper from the International Red Cross in Zagreb came to me saying that my son was alive. Nobody knew what happened to my husband. When this paper was drawn out, he was proclaimed alive. He was taken from the camp as dead. My son has a paper from the Red Cross in Zagreb saying that my son is alive. So here are the documents. Who wrote them, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you would like to show them to the Prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This came from Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- if you would like to show it to the Prosecution afterwards, no doubt, they could make use of them as they think fit, but thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You're welcome. I think that something ought to be done, that this ought to be shown to someone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, of course, the Defence would move to have a copy of those papers if they are to be received by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, if necessary, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The Prosecution can deal with the matter. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know how late the Chamber is thinking of sitting today, but now that we've finished that witness, there remains the issue of the Ribicic statement to be dealt with. Obviously, it's preferable to deal with it as soon as possible, given that Ribicic is spending time preparing his report and so on. His report will probably not be available in a form to be served until the beginning of next week, but I think the underlying principles could be argued out now, if the Court had time to deal with it. That's why Ms. Somers has joined us, because she's been dealing with Dr. Ribicic and is seized of all the detail, rather more at the top of her mind than I am, but I can deal with it on a later date, if you prefer. She won't be here later this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: On Wednesday then, I take it that the plan is that we will not sit. There are no more witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's no more witnesses, and I don't think I'm going to be able to find one at short notice, and in any event, we were warned that the Court might not have any time for us on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is true. So it may be convenient to deal with it, but it's a question of whether we can sit or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we have 20 minutes to deal with these matters. We've got, may I say, to start with the Defence objection, which, summarised, is that this witness was not on the original list, despite various orders being made that witnesses should be notified to the Court and to the Defence, and in fact I think I'm right in saying his name didn't appear until August. That's the objection, and we'll hear from the Prosecution now as to why they say we should allow the witness to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can just deal with the first procedural matter, and Ms. Somers can deal with the detail, I find this an astonishing objection and typical of the desire, simply, to keep any evidence out on any technical ground available to the Defence, however misconceived. Your Honours, I have to say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, maybe, but apart from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because, as I started to explain on the last occasion, this is an issue that was raised well before any deadlines were identified and reached. It was an issue identified by our preparing the constitutional expert in Blaskic's rather complex trial testimony in a reduced and easily consumable form and serving it for admission. That general course is something, I think, of which the Chamber would approve; that is, using evidence that might be admissible from another trial in this one and, indeed, using it in a convenient and compact format. The Defence indicated that they were not prepared to accept that evidence without having the witness here for cross-examination. That witness suffered certain consequences as a result of giving evidence in Blaskic and is, unfortunately, not able to help us. He declines to come, and that may be understandable. I made it plain right from the beginning that I was looking for an alternative. The Defence pre-trial brief, volume 1, on factual issues, the second part of that document, contains something called a "Constitutional Analysis of the Croatian Community and the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna," and although not authored -- at least not publicly authored -- it's plainly the fruits of research that they have undertaken with an expert and which they intend to lay before the Court in due course. Its conclusions, favourable to the Defence, no doubt, are conclusions which they will know already from the way that the expert in Blaskic would have expressed himself, are not conclusions we, for one second, accept. Our efforts to find an appropriate expert met with various difficulties, maybe a general and understandable concern on the part of retained academics -- or academics of the appropriate level of seniority retained in parts of the former Yugoslavia to come to this Tribunal, with all the risks that are associated. Those difficulties were compounded by the fact that it was certainly hoped at one stage and, indeed, was the clearly expressed desire of the Chamber, I think, at one stage that the Prosecution case would end by Christmas. So when we found one expert who was otherwise available and appropriately qualified, but when that deadline emerged as a possible deadline, we had to look elsewhere, and we found the next expert and went through the necessary extended process of negotiating with him and seeing whether he was qualified and whether he was prepared to help. On the 16th of June, at page 4058 of the transcript, I informed the Chamber and, indeed, the Defence of all of this and said: "We have now identified an expert, or I think we have now identified an expert. I'm not sure how long it's going to take for me to have that report." I beg your pardon. That was the previous expert that was not available, but I explained the position that we were still looking and what the problems were, and as soon as I knew of the availability of Dr. Ribicic, on the 5th of August, I explained the position and named him. At none of these intervening explanations by me of our position was any objection expressed. The Defence have suffered no prejudice of any kind because, of course, experts are subject to quite specific rules on disclosure, 21 days before they give evidence, with liberty to the Defence to serve a notice saying that they require to cross-examine the expert; earlier, of course, if the expert's report is available, but by no means is it always the case that they will be, and, indeed, expert reports have been served in this case after the initial deadlines but in accordance with the Tribunal's Rules. So they've suffered no prejudice. They knew we were looking for an expert, they knew of one name that they rejected, and all that's happened is that they've found a name. It may be that the name troubles them because he is a man of great eminence and will be able to assist the Chamber very considerably in analysing the constitutional position of the state and of the body Herceg-Bosna, and he will be able to deal with all those issues raised in the Defence brief. Of course, the Defence brief comes without an identified expert, so we can't begin to analyse the value or otherwise of that report, and we know that the Defence are not prepared to allow experts to be put together so that they can thrash out issues and narrow the issues for the assistance of the Chamber. So we have to do it this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, so that I can have the timetable right, you served, as I recollect, before the trial --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well before the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- but certainly by the beginning, a summary of an expert's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's proposed, is it, that this witness should deal with the same subject?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes, and I shan't then be seeking to read Dr. Pajic's evidence into this trial because they made it clear they want to cross-examine whichever expert we call. But it may be that it would be helpful if you just hear very briefly from Ms. Somers on the detailed issues, because she's been dealing with these matters more than I have, the detailed issues on which this witness can speak, and, indeed, because she's been in contact with him directly, she can probably give you some account of the conclusions that he reaches, radically different from the Defence, which they desire to keep from evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've got five minutes, I'm afraid, Ms. Somers, to do all that.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Pursuant to what Mr. Nice has informed the Court, it is essential, because these issues have been squarely raised by the Defence, that this Court be able to have a clear objective view of the legal structure of what was known as Herceg-Bosna, both in its community form, as it were, and in its republic form. There are mischaracterisations as to the powers of the presidency which form the basis for the Defence position, which this Court must be made aware of, that are central to the issues of guilt or innocence or power of the accused. The particular individual, Dr. Ciril Ribicic, is peculiarly capable of rendering a very definitive position and giving this Court the inside, as it were -- from the inside position understanding of the structures themselves and the context in which they arose, in as much as Dr. Ribicic is a professor of law at Ljubljana University in Slovenia; he is a well-known international and constitutional lawyer; he is a member of parliament of the sovereign state of Slovenia; he, in fact, assisted in drafting the documents which led to sovereignty for Slovenia, the constitutional documents; he is born and bred in the system; he is capable of dealing with the most critical documents in B/C/S, in the language in which they were drafted, as it is one of his first languages, his first language being Slovenian, followed closely by B/C/S; and will be able to lay aside any of the serious mischaracterisations about both the entity and the powers of the accused. As Mr. Nice had indicated, it was extremely difficult to try to get a person of this calibre to commit to time. He has been very generous with us in so doing, and we would hope very much that this Chamber will be able to benefit strongly from his evidence. The position itself must be addressed because it is so central to the -- I would say it is a core issue of this case. If there are any particular questions about Dr. Ribicic that I can answer for the Chamber, I would be very happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not going to waste time by belabouring the points already made in the skeleton argument that we filed. Those arguments speak for themselves. The fact of the matter is that today, we stand before you without a statement from Mr. Ribicic. We didn't know whether he was a fact or an expert witness as of August the 5th, but apparently that issue has now been resolved. We don't have a summary of what his testimony is purported to be, and the Court's orders speak with a very simple, clear precision that does not need to be beaten to death. All of the witness statements of the witnesses that the Prosecution intends to call had to be delivered to the Defence by no later than May the 17th, after two separate extensions, and the fact of the matter is that the statement or summary of this witness has not been delivered to us. On the subject of the constitutional discussion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Sayers, regarding this particular point you are talking about, the Chamber's order, it has to do with the list of witnesses, such as it existed, and the statements of those witnesses. You certainly know that it is possible to review that list of witnesses, and if a modification of that list is authorised by the Chamber, then the Prosecutor is allowed to produce statements. So we cannot say that because there is no statement that we cannot call a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: You're quite correct, of course, Your Honour, that Rule 73 permits the Prosecution to reinstate its list of witnesses with the permission of the Trial Chamber, provided there is good reason for doing that, obviously, and we would submit that given the fact that there have been two separate extensions here, there is no good reason for that. Actually, turning to the specifics of the application, since it deals with the discussion on the constitutionality of the institutions of Herceg-Bosna that was contained in our opening brief, I must say I'm extremely flattered that the Prosecution deemed that a constitutional expert was necessary to write those portions of the brief, but with all due respect, I don't qualify for that. I actually wrote those sections myself, and we didn't have any constitutional expert. Frankly, all it is is a legal analysis of the documents themselves, and that's exactly what Dr. Pajic testified about for about four or five days in the Blaskic case, just the legal import of documents. That's what our analysis confined itself to, and, frankly, the Court itself is -- that's what the job of the Court is, to define or to discern what the meaning of documents may be. That's something that's peculiarly within the province of the Court and outside the province, I would submit, of any constitutional expert. In addition, we've let the Prosecution know what our position is from the very beginning. I wrote a letter to Mr. Nice, I believe, or Mr. Scott on the 17th of June of this year that says, "We shall object, when necessary, to any attempt by the Prosecution to introduce testimony or statements from witnesses whose statements have not been provided to us prior to the court or the deadline. We believe that this is not an unreasonable position, given the extremely large witness list assembled by the Prosecution."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, if you are, in fact, provided now in a timely manner with the statement of the witness so that you can study it and decide what your position is, what prejudice would there be to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Well, the prejudice is as follows, Your Honour: First of all, there is a clear Court order, and it simply hasn't been complied with, and that's the first position. The second position is that the Prosecution, as I gather, is saying that the testimony of this gentleman is going to be completely duplicative of the testimony that has already been introduced through Mr. Pajic in the Blaskic case, and it seems to me that this is just a completely unnecessary waste of time, especially since we are coming up to the end of the Prosecution's case, at least I hope, by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, I'm sorry to interrupt, but let me follow the argument. Are you saying that if Dr. Pajic's evidence was introduced or somebody sought to do that, you wouldn't object?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I think that that's an extremely terse way of putting it, yes, Your Honour. It seems to me that if his testimony has already been taken, in the interests of saving time and not consuming the Court's resources with a live witness who would no doubt testify for yet more days, we would be prepared to reconsider our position with respect to Pajic, provided that's not deemed to be a blanket waiver of our previously-articulated position. Really, that's all I have to say on the matter, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that of any use?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, I'm afraid not, Your Honour, because we've moved on from there. This witness, who has already been seen, holds his own views which in some ways are similar to and in some ways may be different from Pajic. But more important, he deals quite specifically with the role of Kordic. Pajic, at the time we were looking at that, deals with things much more generally. So it's extremely important that he comes in and gives evidence himself. He was identified as an expert on the 5th of August. There's no question of his being a fact witness. The report or the summary contained in the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice, you are presenting your argument. I'd like to understand it, but I don't understand it very well. You told us that this witness will be talking about Kordic, whereas the previous one spoke about Blaskic. If I understood well, it would be an expert testimony on the presidency of Herceg-Bosna. That is what I read in the transcript, the presidency of Herceg-Bosna, both as a community and as a republic. So these are the people involved. We are not listening to an expert opinion on constitutional law, apparently, but on the community of Herceg-Bosna, its nature, its legal characteristics. Therefore, your argument about the personalities involved, I don't see how that changes anything regarding the nature of that community.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Quite right, insofar as the individual personalities are concerned, but so far as a person who is the office holder of the office of vice-president, the constitutional position is important. What I intended to say, and I haven't got the transcript before me to know whether I achieved it, what I intended to say was that in Blaskic, matters were looked at much more generally. In Kordic, they'll have to be looked at generally but also in relation to Kordic's role, he being an office holder. But in addition to that, there's, I suppose, the reality that this witness, and Ms. Somers may be able to helped you more on this, may hold slightly different views from those of the witness in Blaskic, and he, having been seen and spoken to, is the witness who could most help -- it is thought could most help the Chamber in relation to the facts of this trial. I'm also surprised at the thought that what is contained in the factual brief of the Defence is drafted purely by a lawyer, because it has all the form, with conclusions and so on, as if it's drafted by somebody who would be familiar both with the language and with the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we'll be able to look at that in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The report itself, as I say, should be available in about ten days, the beginning of next week I would hope, and as Ms. Somers has already indicated, it deals with a number of central issues on the legality or illegality as well as the nature of the powers of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Ms. Somers, can you say whether the evidence of this expert witness will differ from the evidence given by Pajic in Blaskic?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Dr. Pajic's testimony dealt with a very detailed analysis of the Gazette, the Official Gazette of Herceg-Bosna, the Narodni list. This witness incorporates, of course, that type of analysis in the same type of detail but is responsive to the very specific issues raised by the Defence in the characterisation of the types of powers that would be consistent with the vice-president, as an officer of the presidency. The position taken by the Defence is that it was a strictly legislative role and that all of the types of activity that the Prosecution has proven to date and intends to prove in the future would be inconsistent and is essentially a mischaracterization by the Prosecution. In fact, the type of understanding which this Chamber can receive from Dr. Ribicic will make it more than clear just what the various positions entailed. It will also make very clear what Herceg-Bosna represented to the Republic of Croatia, as well as to its impact on the then continuously sovereign state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is a great deal in common, certainly, but because the issues framed by the Defence go beyond the Pajic area, all of which, by the way, was completely given to the Defence in the form of the summary, so in fact a summary was certainly presented, so this would be Pajic plus, based on the issues framed by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Somers, I should like to follow on to the question that has just been put to you by my colleague, Judge Robinson. I do not need to remind you that in this Tribunal, we are confronted with a problem of time and we are trying to be as speedy as possible while, of course, fully meeting all the requirements of justice, and we're always asking you to assist us. Is it possible, in this case, in accordance with what you have just said, to have the transcript of the witness Pajic as he testified in the Blaskic case, when he provided legal expertise on the community of Herceg-Bosna, and to bring Mr. Ribicic only for the aspects that do not appear in the Blaskic transcript, because that would meet your concerns, the concerns of the Prosecution. I don't know whether the Defence could also assist us by agreeing to this, because I think in this way we would have a clearer idea of the legal aspects and the constitutional aspects of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think that that would be a sound resolution. I would also ask, of course, that the Court accept, pursuant to Rule 94 bis, the statement which is being prepared and shall be ready for the Chamber by Dr. Ribicic so that the areas which are not well dealt with by Dr. Pajic may be presented fully and fairly to the Chamber, and then perhaps any cross-examination or questions from the Bench could be crafted accordingly. But I think it would serve best if you had the Ribicic statement as well as the Pajic one, and what the Defence and Chamber do with it, of course, is certainly within his or her own judgement as appropriate. Is that responsive, Judge Bennouna? I think it would be helpful, of course, to have the Pajic material, much of which will be recognisable in the Ribicic statement, but there are other issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we have to decide, first of all, whether the evidence of Dr. Ribicic would be admissible at this stage. Then, no doubt, we could go on to decide how precisely we can deal with it in order not to waste time. What we don't want is a lot of evidence which is given twice, when it can be done more shortly. We'll consider this for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We shall reject the motion and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We shall reject the motion. We shall not exclude this witness's evidence. Rule 73 bis(E) permits the Prosecutor, if it's in the interests of justice, to file a motion allowing her to vary a decision as to which witnesses are to be called. In this particular case, from the outset there has been a clear indication that evidence of this type and dealing with this issue would be called. We accept that there has been difficulties in finding an expert, as there sometimes are in this particular field in this particular region, and in those circumstances we think that as much notice as can be given has been given. The Defence will suffer no prejudice or unfairness as a result of calling this witness, provided, of course, that the Rules as to proper notice of expert evidence are given and that they have the time in which to consider the document before being called upon to cross-examine or make a decision about it. In those circumstances, although it's right that in other cases we have refused any extra or additional evidence, those related to fact witnesses, as I recall, in this particular case we think it's in the interests of justice to allow the witness to be called. I may finally add this: How the witness is to be called, having regard to the other evidence on the topic, we can perhaps leave for consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we separate until, I think, next Monday, and while the last witness's testimony is in mind, and in particular the documents she produced right at the end, I'm in a position to tell the Chamber and, indeed, to show to the Chamber, if they want it, and certainly to my friends for the defendants, that what she produced were two certificates, two International Committee of the Red Cross certificates, covering the detention and release of her two relations, husband and son. I don't think that they conflict with the evidence that she's given. She may have misunderstood the documents herself, but I'll show them to Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now, and the Court will sit again next Monday, half past 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 5.24 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 11th day of October, 1999, at 9.30 a.m. 23 24 25
